rationale: The numbers I was handed look like a wonderful business: a 5-year average ROE of 30.6%, debt-to-equity of 0.497, and a 40.4% margin of safety against an intrinsic value of $1,271.73 per share. But I have been burned by pretty spreadsheets before. The snapshot gives me no ten-year earnings record, no ROIC, no management or insider data and no measured evidence of the moat, and the valuation leans on 8% growth discounted at 5%. Debt-to-equity sits right at the 0.5 line, with no cushion. A cheap price doesn't make up for the checks I couldn't perform, so I'll sit on my hands, keep this on the list, and wait for the missing facts. Position size is zero for now.

exit_trigger: Not applicable - no position. I would revisit only on evidence of a durable moat, such as demonstrated pricing power and consistent earnings across ten years, at a price with at least a 15% margin of safety.
rationale: I understand the business: Best Buy sells consumer electronics through big stores and online, and it earns its money on the markup. The numbers in front of me look decent, with a 20.6% margin of safety and a debt-to-equity of 0.39. But a discount is not a moat, and I can't find one here. A seller of other people's branded gadgets, in a category where customers compare prices on their phones, has to rebuild its edge every year, and I have no evidence of pricing power in this snapshot. I also can't check ten years of earnings or the management record from what I was given. When in doubt I say no, and I'll wait for a business whose advantage doesn't depend on the next product cycle.

exit_trigger: Evidence of eroding pricing power or declining same-store sales; Large competitors replicating the format and compressing margins; Management destroying value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value on a persistent basis
rationale: Sprouts Farmers Market is a grocery store, and I understand grocers well enough. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 27.8%, a debt-to-equity of 0.0, and a price of $53.47 against an intrinsic value estimate of $104.13, a 48.6% margin of safety. That is eye-catching, but I won't lean on a number I can't check: the snapshot gives me no ten-year earnings record, no management or capital-allocation detail, and no evidence on what moat a specialty grocer really has. The zero debt figure is also suspicious, because the snapshot does not say whether leases are counted, and a company with untagged debt is not a company without debt. The discount rate of 5% is also generous, so the valuation is sensitive to it. Until I can verify consistent earnings and that the moat is real rather than a fad in healthy eating, I watch from the sidelines. It is better to wait for the pitch in my sweet spot than to swing at one I can't see clearly.

rationale: The numbers in front of me are handsome: 5-year average ROE of 34.6%, a reported debt-to-equity of 0.0, and a market cap of about $11.6 billion. A brand that has to win each season with new product is a moat that must be rebuilt continuously, and I've said those are no moats at all. The snapshot gives no 10-year earnings record, no management tenure or capital allocation history, and no evidence of pricing power or customer retention, so I can't verify what I'd need. I'll pass and wait for a pitch squarely in my sweet spot.

exit_trigger: Evidence that the brands can no longer raise prices without losing volume (moat erosion); Private-label or competitor share gains that compress margins persistently; Management capital allocation that destroys value, such as overpriced acquisitions or leverage-funded buybacks; Disclosure that debt is materially larger than the reported debt-to-equity of 0.10 implies; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting
rationale: The numbers in front of me are attractive: a price of $21.75 against an intrinsic value of $43.71 per share, a 50.25% margin of safety, a 5-year average ROE of 21.66%, and debt-to-equity of 0.10. But the model behind that value assumes 0% growth at a 5% discount rate, and a cheap price on a mediocre business is the cigar-butt trap I outgrew with See's Candies. I cannot verify from this snapshot the 10-year earnings record, CEO tenure and capital allocation, the evidence of pricing power, or whether the low debt figure captures all the debt. Missing evidence is not a pass, so I will not buy on the fields that happen to be present. I will put this on the watch list and complete the homework on the brand's pricing power and the earnings history before I commit capital.

exit_trigger: Evidence that pricing power or gross margins are eroding versus larger or online distributors; Sustained decline in ROE well below the 15% threshold without a clear one-time cause; Debt-to-equity rising materially above 0.5; Management destroying value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Price rising above 1.5x intrinsic value with no improvement in fundamentals
rationale: MSM distributes industrial and metalworking supplies, a business I can explain in two paragraphs. The numbers in front of me look good: a 5-year average ROE of 20.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.35, and a price about 23% below a $157 intrinsic value estimate. But that estimate leans on 8% growth, a capped trailing CAGR of 9%, discounted at only 5%, and the owner earnings of about $303 million are only 4.5% of the $6.76 billion market cap. The snapshot tells me nothing about ten years of earnings consistency, management tenure, capital allocation, or evidence of pricing power against larger distributors and online sellers. I won't buy a moat I can't verify just because the arithmetic looks pleasant, so I'm watching and waiting for those answers or a fatter margin of safety.

exit_trigger: Evidence that pricing power is eroding, such as sustained price cuts or share loss to lower-cost rivals; Technological change that makes the installed product line or distribution relationships obsolete; Capital allocation failures, such as large acquisitions at poor returns or buybacks at prices well above intrinsic value; Return on equity falling persistently below 15% or leverage rising above 0.5 debt-to-equity; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persistent
rationale: A. O. Smith makes water heaters and related products, and I can explain that in two paragraphs. The numbers I was given are the kind I like: a five-year average ROE of 23.7%, debt-to-equity of 0.083, a $9.04 billion market cap, and a 33% margin of safety against an intrinsic value of $95.72 on a price of $64.10. But I am not going to buy on the fields that happen to be present. This snapshot has no ten-year earnings record, no CEO tenure or capital allocation history, and no measured evidence of pricing power or market share, and I treat a check I cannot perform as a check not passed. The valuation also leans on 8% growth against a 5% discount rate. The owner-earnings yield on today's market cap is only about 5.2%, so the margin of safety depends heavily on that growth assumption. I will keep it on the watch list and wait until the missing evidence is in hand. Being patient costs little, while a mistake costs a lot.
